Feed small live and frozen foods such as Artemia nauplii, Moina and grindal worm plus finely sized dried foods.
Tannin-stained water from bogwood or leaf litter helps replicate its natural still, blackwater habitat.
A hardy, inexpensive and peaceful shoaling tetra that is an excellent choice for community aquariums and beginners.
Keep a group of at least 6, ideally 10 or more, to reduce shyness and encourage natural schooling.
Feeds readily on small live and frozen foods such as bloodworm, Daphnia and brine shrimp alongside dried flakes and granules.
Compatible with livebearers, danios, rasboras, other tetras and peaceful bottom dwellers like Corydoras.
Keep in a group of at least 8-10 as it is a shy shoaling species that colours up best in numbers.
Only add to a mature, stable aquarium as it is sensitive to elevated nitrate and water-quality swings.
Provide a densely planted tank with some water flow and a darker substrate to show off the neon-green colour.
Feed small live and frozen foods such as Daphnia and Artemia alongside fine dried foods.
A tiny, timid nano fish best kept in a group of 8-10 in a quiet, densely planted blackwater-style tank.
Prefers soft, acidic water with gentle filtration, leaf litter and dim lighting.
Do not add to a biologically immature tank as it is sensitive to water-chemistry fluctuations.
Offer small live and frozen foods; its tiny mouth needs finely crushed dried foods.
A hardy, beginner-friendly shoaling danio best kept in a group of 8-10 for calm behaviour and best colour.
Use a tight-fitting lid as these active fish are accomplished jumpers.
Tolerates cooler temperatures and a wide pH range, making it well suited to unheated or subtropical setups.
An unfussy eater that takes quality dried foods supplemented with live and frozen fare.
Keep in a densely planted tank with dark substrate to reduce skittishness.
Prefers neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately hard water and will not thrive in acidic conditions.
Buy the largest group possible (ideally 15-20+) so rival-male sparring is diffused across the shoal.
Newly imported fish often need small live or frozen foods such as Daphnia and Artemia before accepting dried foods.
Provide soft, acidic, mineral-poor water in a heavily planted, dimly lit forest-stream setup.
Filtration can be gentle since it comes from sluggish waters.
Keep a group of at least 8-10 and avoid boisterous tankmates that outcompete it for food.
Offer small live and frozen foods alongside quality dried foods for best condition and colour.
A hardy, adaptable schooling barb well suited to beginner community tanks.
Keep 8-10 or more so males display their best colours and fish are less skittish.
Decorate with driftwood and some floating plants, and provide moderate filter flow.
Feed a varied omnivorous diet of small live/frozen foods plus good quality flakes and granules.
A very large, active shoaling barb that needs an expansive tank of at least 2 metres length with powerful filtration.
Keep in groups of six or more to reduce skittishness and curb nipping behaviour.
Largely herbivorous, so offer plenty of vegetable matter alongside quality dried and frozen foods.
Will eat small tankmates and uproots or eats soft plants, so choose robust companions and hardy vegetation.
Requires a mature tank with strong current (15-20x turnover) and high oxygenation to mimic fast hillstream conditions.
Prefers cooler water and struggles in warm, poorly oxygenated aquaria.
Feeds mainly on benthic algae grazed from surfaces, supplemented with vegetable foods and occasional live/frozen items.
Keep a group of six or more to observe natural behaviour; males are territorial but not brutally aggressive.
A gregarious loach that should be kept in groups of at least five or six, preferably ten or more, for confident behaviour.
Needs mature, stable water with spotless conditions and regular 30-50% weekly water changes.
Largely carnivorous, taking bloodworm, Daphnia and Artemia, plus quality dried foods and some vegetable matter.
Generally peaceful but can nip long, flowing fins, so avoid slow long-finned tankmates.
subspeciesNote: Formerly classified as Botia and Yasuhikotakia sidthimunki; older references use those genus names.

notes: A temperate species that prefers cooler water (18-24 C) and is not suited to warm tropical tanks long-term.
Provide a soft sand or fine-gravel substrate as it likes to burrow and bury itself.
Keep the tank tightly covered, as this loach is an active jumper and reacts to weather changes.
Peaceful but may eat eggs, fry, or very small tankmates; more relaxed when kept with a few conspecifics.
One of the smallest loaches in the hobby (~3 cm), ideal for well-planted nano aquariums.
Keep in a group of at least 8-10 with both sexes to bring out colour and minimise any bullying.
Provide a soft substrate they can sift through and gentle flow with plenty of plant cover.
Offer small foods such as micro-pellets, frozen bloodworm, Daphnia, and brine shrimp.
subspeciesNote: Undescribed species; also historically sold as Yunnanilus sp. 'rosy'.

notes: A hardy, very peaceful schooling fish well suited to community and beginner setups.
Keep in a group of 8-10 or more to reduce nervousness and encourage natural shoaling.
Colours show best over a dark substrate in a planted tank with dim lighting and gentle filtration.
Feed a varied diet of small live/frozen foods (Daphnia, Artemia) alongside quality dried foods.
Requires hard, alkaline water; soft or acidic conditions cause rapid health decline.
Predominantly a plant-eater, so include vegetable matter such as blanched spinach or veggie flake.
Keep in trios of two females to one male, as mature males can be aggressive toward each other and smaller fish.
Provide open swimming space alongside densely planted areas for this active swimmer.
A peaceful, hardy fish well suited to a general hard-water community aquarium.
Prefers moderately hard or harder water and does poorly in soft, acidic conditions.
Keep more females than males so the relentless attention of males is spread out.
Accepts most frozen, live, or dried foods and appreciates a planted setup.
One of the world's smallest fish; best kept as a peaceful species-only colony in a small planted tank.
Keep water flow to a minimum with gentle filtration among dense vegetation.
Accepts most foods but favors small live or frozen items like brine shrimp and Daphnia plus some vegetable matter.
Tolerates a wider hardness range than mollies/platies but still prefers neutral-to-alkaline water.
A surface-dwelling micropredator best fed small live or frozen foods such as Artemia, Daphnia and bloodworms alongside dried foods.
Males can be aggressive toward each other, so provide dense planting and refuges, and keep 2-3 females per male in a harem.
Undemanding as to water chemistry within a soft-to-moderately-hard, near-neutral range, making it a good first killifish.
A capable jumper that requires a tightly-fitting, gap-free cover.
subspeciesNote: Several colour forms/subspecies (e.g. nigerianus) exist with similar requirements.

notes: A voracious surface predator that will eat any tankmate or dwarf shrimp small enough to fit in its mouth, so choose companions carefully.
Feeds readily on meaty live and frozen foods (bloodworms, brine shrimp, Daphnia) and larger dried foods.
An accomplished jumper, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.
Hardy and adaptable across soft-to-moderately-hard, slightly acidic to neutral water.
A tiny, peaceful nano surface micropredator best kept in a group of at least 8-10 for confident, natural behaviour.
Prefers soft, acidic water in a heavily planted, dimly lit tank and should only be added to a biologically mature aquarium.
Requires small foods such as Artemia nauplii, Daphnia and grindal worms; its tiny upturned mouth cannot manage large pellets.
Too small and delicate for boisterous community tanks despite its peaceful nature.
Tiny, delicate species best kept in a group of 6+ (ideally 10 or more) in a densely planted, mature aquarium with gentle flow.
Vulnerable to fin-nipping and outcompetition for food, so avoid boisterous or fast-feeding tankmates.
Feed small live and frozen foods such as Daphnia, Moina and Artemia nauplii plus finely crushed floating dry food.
Males need open swimming space to display their elongated fins to females.
Peaceful, small shoaling rainbowfish best kept in groups of 6-8+ with a ratio of 2-3 females per male to encourage male displays.
Requires hard, alkaline water (pH 7-8, 10-25 dGH); does poorly in soft acidic conditions.
Offer varied dried, frozen and live foods to bring out the blue-green body colour and yellow fins.
Provide open swimming lanes between planted areas where displaying males can spar.
Active, peaceful schooling fish that needs a group of at least 8-10 and plenty of open swimming space with strong, well-oxygenated flow.
Keep in hard, neutral-to-alkaline water; true B. geayi prefers cooler temperatures (around 20-24C) than most tropical community fish.
Feed small live and frozen foods (bloodworm, Daphnia, Artemia) alongside good-quality flakes and granules.
A robust swimmer that can outcompete slow or timid tankmates at feeding time.
subspeciesNote: Fish sold as Bedotia geayi are commonly the similar Bedotia madagascariensis, which tolerate warmer 23-32C and grow larger.

notes: Requires very soft, acidic, warm water (pH 4.0-6.5, near-zero hardness) and is highly intolerant of poor water quality.
A shy micropredator that must be fed small live or frozen foods such as Artemia nauplii, Daphnia and grindal/micro worms.
Keep in a group of at least six, as isolated fish become stressed and pine.
House only with small, peaceful, slow-moving tankmates in a densely planted, dimly lit tank.
A hardy, adaptable labyrinth fish that tolerates a wide range of water conditions and accepts most prepared, frozen and live foods.
Generally peaceful but males can become territorial toward each other and other gouramis, so give plenty of space.
Skittish by nature; provide a planted tank with open swimming areas, slow flow and floating cover.
As an air-breather it needs regular access to the surface, so leave a gap between the water and the lid.
subspeciesNote: Genus Trichopodus was formerly Trichogaster; older sources list this as Trichogaster microlepis.

notes: One of the largest and most peaceful gouramis, reaching about 25-30 cm, so it needs a long tank of 180 litres or more.
Feeds mainly on plant matter, algae and phytoplankton but also takes invertebrates and prepared foods.
Males are relatively non-territorial compared with other gouramis and it makes a good community fish with similarly sized, peaceful species.
May eat very small fish, so choose tankmates of appropriate size.
subspeciesNote: Genus Trichopodus was formerly Trichogaster; older sources list this as Trichogaster pectoralis.

notes: A shy, retiring cichlid that settles best with dither fish and plenty of cover such as wood and broad-leaved plants.
Sensitive to poor water quality and prone to head-and-lateral-line erosion, so only add to a mature tank with regular water changes.
Monogamous biparental substrate spawner that becomes only mildly territorial when breeding.
Feeds on prepared foods plus live/frozen bloodworm, Artemia and Daphnia.
One of the most peaceful Central American cichlids, suitable for a robust community with medium tetras, barbs and catfish.
Prefers a sandy substrate with rocks, wood and flowerpots for cover, plus clean water kept low in nitrate.
A grazer in nature; feed cichlid pellets supplemented with spirulina/vegetable flake and occasional live or frozen foods.
Becomes territorial around a chosen flat spawning site when breeding, with both parents guarding eggs and fry.
subspeciesNote: Also classified as Herotilapia multispinosa; older literature lists it under that name.

notes: A large but generally mild-mannered cichlid for spacious, peaceful South American community tanks.
Grows quickly and needs an appropriately large tank from the start, with soft, slightly acidic water.
Behaves best kept with conspecifics; lone specimens can turn aggressive as they mature.
Omnivorous and unfussy, taking dried foods, meatier fare like bloodworm and prawn, plus some vegetable matter.
Best kept as a single male with one or more females (harem) in a well-planted tank with caves and leaf litter.
Wild specimens need soft, acidic water (pH below 6.5, low dGH); commercially bred fish are more tolerant.
Primarily carnivorous; feed live or frozen Artemia, Daphnia and bloodworm, supplemented with quality micro-pellets.
Males can be territorial toward each other, so keep a single dominant male per small tank.
A Lake Malawi mbuna requiring hard, alkaline water and a rocky aquascape with many caves and territories.
Highly aggressive toward conspecifics; keep a large group of 12 or more to diffuse aggression rather than a pair.
Grazes on algae/aufwuchs, so feed a spirulina-based herbivore diet and avoid protein-rich foods that cause bloat.
Do not house with other blue-barred mbuna, as similar-looking species trigger intense fighting.

notes: A Lake Malawi peacock needing hard, alkaline water with an open sandy substrate for sifting and rockwork for cover.
Keep one colourful male with several females to spread out his attention and reduce harassment.
In the wild it sifts sand for invertebrates, so offer a carnivore/insectivore diet of frozen and quality pellet foods.
More peaceful than mbuna, but males become territorial at breeding time; avoid mixing with other peacock species.
A shoaling species that is far more active and confident when kept in a group of five or more.
Peaceful toward similar-sized tankmates but will eat any fish small enough to swallow, so avoid tiny companions.
Its long, sharp pectoral and dorsal spines tangle easily in nets, so handle with a container rather than a net.
Provide a soft sand substrate and plenty of open swimming space for this fast, active swimmer.
A peaceful, gregarious bottom-dweller that must be kept in a group of six or more to feel secure.
Use a soft sand or smooth rounded gravel substrate to protect its delicate sensory barbels.
Feed a varied omnivorous diet of sinking pellets, wafers, and frozen foods that reach the bottom.
True C. julii shows fine discrete black spots, unlike the connected reticulations of the often-confused C. trilineatus.
subspeciesNote: Most 'julii' sold are actually Corydoras trilineatus, which has net-like reticulations rather than distinct spots.

notes: Totally unaggressive toward tankmates but nocturnal and will swallow any fish small enough to fit in its mouth.
Its serrated pectoral spines lock outward and snag nets badly, so move it in a rigid container.
Provide caves, driftwood, or PVC pipe as daytime hiding spots since it is shy and mostly active after dark.
Offer sinking pellets or wafers as a staple, supplemented with bloodworms and small earthworms.
A peaceful, slow-moving bottom-dweller ideal as an introduction to keeping and breeding Loricariid catfish.
Use a soft sandy substrate with driftwood and plenty of hiding places to help it feel secure.
Feed sinking dried foods plus vegetables like courgette and spinach, supplemented with occasional bloodworm or daphnia.
Keep with peaceful tankmates as vigorous species will easily outcompete it for food.
A delicate algae grazer that requires a mature, established tank with abundant biofilm and pristine, well-oxygenated water.
The bulk of its diet must be vegetable matter such as algae wafers, cucumber and blanched spinach.
Extremely sensitive to poor or deteriorating water quality, so only add to a stable system.
Prefers gentle flow and clings to driftwood, plant leaves and tank surfaces.
A surface-dwelling ambush predator that will eat any fish small enough to fit in its upturned mouth.
An exceptional jumper that requires a tight-fitting, gap-free lid to prevent escape.
Feed floating foods such as live or frozen insects, crickets and shrimp taken from the water surface.
Provide dim lighting, floating plants and minimal water movement in soft, slightly acidic water.
